The shipped example shows the\n14\tshape of the problem: `example/weather-tool.ts` declares `location` as a required string, then\n15\tcasts and defaults it (`(input.location as string) || 'Unknown'`) with a comment warning the reader\n16\tthat `inputSchema` shapes what the model sends but does not enforce it. That is the careful version,\n17\twritten by the people who wrote the engine — and it still answers a malformed call with a\n18\tconfidently formatted forecast for `'Unknown'` rather than telling the model it got the call wrong.\n19\t\n20\tThe registry currently pushes this check onto each tool's own executor, leaving every consumer\n21\tto implement it itself — differently each time, or not at all. Validation enforces `required`, declared types and `enum` only —\n41\tit does not inject `additionalProperties: false`, coerce types, or apply defaults, and\n42\tthere is no opt-out flag.\n43\t\n44\tUpdate `docs/adding-a-tool.md`, `README.md` and `.specify/spec.md` to match.\n45\t\n46\t## Acceptance criteria\n47\t\n48\t- [ ] `ToolRegistry.execute` validates `input` against the resolved definition's\n49\t      `inputSchema` before calling the executor; on failure it returns a `ToolResponse`\n50\t      whose `result` describes the failure, and the executor is never invoked\n51\t- [ ] A new `src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts` (the registry has no test file today)\n52\t      registers a tool requiring a `location` string, calls `execute` with `{}`, and\n53\t      asserts the returned result names `location` as required and the executor's call\n54\t      count is `0`\n55\t- [ ] A test asserts valid input with an unlisted extra property is passed through to the\n56\t      executor unchanged (`toEqual`, so an added default or coerced value fails the test) —\n57\t      exactly once\n58\t- [ ] A test asserts a wrong-typed field (a number where a string is required) is rejected\n59\t      with a message naming the field path and the expected type, and that the message does\n60\t      **not** contain the offending value\n61\t- [ ] A test asserts `register` throws at registration time for an uncompilable schema, and\n62\t      that the thrown message names the tool\n63\t- [ ] A test asserts a function-valued tool definition whose returned schema differs between\n64\t      calls is validated against the schema current at that call, not a stale cached one\n65\t- [ ] A test asserts a static tool's schema is compiled once across ten `execute` calls\n66\t- [ ] A tool-loop test in `chatOrchestrator.test.ts` drives a stub provider through a\n67\t      rejected tool call followed by a corrected retry, and asserts `processMessage`\n68\t      resolves — not rejects — with the rejection text visible to the provider on the next\n69\t      round\n70\t- [ ] `execute` still throws `Unknown tool: <name>` for an unregistered name, unchanged,\n71\t      pinned by a test\n72\t- [ ] Rejection messages and log lines name the failing property paths and the constraint\n73\t      that failed, and never a property **value**. []);\n  }\n\n  has(name: string): boolean {\n    return this.tools.has(name);\n  }\n\n  async execute(name: string, input: Record<string, unknown>, context?: ToolContext): Promise<ToolResponse> {\n    const tool = this.tools.get(name);\n    if (!tool) {\n      log.warn('tool', 'tool not found', {name});\n      throw new Error(`Unknown tool: ${name}`);\n    }\n    log.info('tool', 'executing', {name, inputKeys: Object.keys(input)});\n    const rawResult = await tool.execute(input, context);\n    const response = normalizeToolResponse(rawResult);\n    log.info('tool', 'execution complete', {\n      name,\n      rawType: typeof rawResult,\n      clientMessageCount: response.clientMessages?.length ?? 0,\n      clientMessageTypes: response.clientMessages?.map(m => m.type) ?? [],\n      suppressAssistantResponse: response.suppressAssistantResponse ?? false,\n    });\n    return response;\n  }\n}\n","numLines":95,"startLine":1,"totalLines":95}},"tool_result_meta":[{"id":"call_f44e789535bf4bc088c39526","permission_decision":{"decision":"accept","source":"config","reason_type":"mode"}}]}

The client never sees the result -- it only sees the tool invocation (name and input parameters). This is fine for most tools, but sometimes a tool knows exactly what to show the user and does not need the AI to rephrase it.\n\nThe `ToolResponse` interface gives tools two additional capabilities:\n\n1. **Client messages** -- send one or more WebSocket messages directly to the client\n2. **Suppress the AI response** -- keep the model's reply in conversation context but hide it from the client\n\nThese are opt-in. Tools that return a plain string continue to work exactly as before.\n\n## The ToolResponse Interface\n\n<!-- doc-block: src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts#ToolResponse -->\n```typescript\ninterface ToolResponse {\n  result: string;\n  clientMessages?: OutgoingMessage[];\n  suppressAssistantResponse?: boolean;\n}\n```\n\n| Field | Purpose |\n|-------|---------|\n| `result` | The string the AI model sees -- identical to what a plain-string executor returns |\n| `clientMessages` | Optional array of `OutgoingMessage` values sent directly to the client via WebSocket |\n| `suppressAssistantResponse` | When `true`, the AI's next text response still accumulates in `session.entries` for context continuity, but is not sent to the client |\n\nA `ToolExecutor` can return either a plain `string` or a `ToolResponse`:\n\n<!-- doc-block: src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts#ToolExecutor -->\n```typescript\ntype ToolExecutor = (input: Record<string, unknown>, context?: ToolContext) => Promise<string | ToolResponse>;\n```\n\n`context` carries the session the call belongs to -- `userId`, `sessionId`, `workspaceId`, and the `authHeaders` forwarded from the WebSocket upgrade, so a tool can proxy the caller's credentials upstream.\n\nThe registry normalizes both forms internally via `normalizeToolResponse()`, so downstream code always sees a `ToolResponse`.\n\n## When to Use This\n\n**Client messages** make sense when the tool result is self-explanatory and the AI does not need to interpret it for the user. A unit conversion, a status update, a formatted data table -- these are cases where the tool knows the best presentation and the AI would just parrot the same information.\n\n**Suppression** pairs naturally with client messages. If the tool already sent the answer to the client, the AI's follow-up (\"The conversion result is 160.93 km\") adds no value. Suppression hides that echo while keeping it in the conversation so the AI remembers the context for follow-up questions.\n\nUse plain string returns (the default) when the AI needs to interpret or summarize the tool result for the user. Database lookups and search results are good examples -- the raw data benefits from the AI explaining it in context.\n\n## Data Flow\n\n```\nPlain string:    executor returns \"data\"\n                   -> normalizeToolResponse wraps to {result: \"data\"}\n                   -> orchestrator feeds result to AI\n                   -> AI responds, client sees the response\n\nWith client messages:\n                 executor returns {result, clientMessages, suppressAssistantResponse}\n                   -> orchestrator extracts .result for AI (unchanged)\n                   -> orchestrator yields tool_result chunk carrying clientMessages\n                   -> if suppress, orchestrator yields suppress_output chunk\n                   -> messageHandler sends clientMessages to client\n                   -> messageHandler blanks pre-tool assistant entries (entry_upsert with empty content)\n                   -> messageHandler skips WebSocket sends for suppressed entries\n                   -> messageHandler sends entry_skip for each new suppressed entry\n                   -> suppressed entries still accumulate in session.entries\n                   -> client adjusts incoming indices using tracked skip list\n```\n\nThe key insight: suppressed entries are invisible to the client but visible to the AI. The conversation context stays intact, so the model can reference previous tool results even when the user did not see the AI's commentary on them.\n\n## Example: Unit Converter\n\nThe `convert_units` tool demonstrates all three features: client messages, suppression, and index assignment. A conversion like \"100 miles to kilometers\" has a definitive answer -- the AI does not need to elaborate.\n\n<!-- doc-block: none -- a simplified tool, marked simplified in its own first line -->\n```typescript\n// src/orchestration/tools/unitConverterTool.ts (simplified)\n\nexport const executeUnitConverter: ToolExecutor = async (input) => {\n  const value = input.value as number;\n  const fromUnit = (input.from_unit as string) || '';\n  const toUnit = (input.to_unit as string) || '';\n\n  const result = convert(value, fromUnit, toUnit);\n\n  if (!result) {\n    // Error case: return plain string so AI can explain the problem\n    return JSON.stringify({error: `Cannot convert from \"${fromUnit}\" to \"${toUnit}\".`});\n  }\n\n  return {\n    result: JSON.stringify({value, fromUnit, toUnit, converted: result.converted, formatted: result.formatted}),\n    clientMessages: [\n      {\n        type: 'entry_upsert',\n        index: 0,\n        entry: {role: 'assistant', content: result.formatted, timestamp: new Date().toISOString(), isStreaming: false},\n      },\n    ],\n    suppressAssistantResponse: true,\n  };\n};\n```\n\nNotice three things:\n\n1. On success, the executor returns a `clientMessages` array with an `entry_upsert` containing the formatted result. The client receives this as an assistant entry. The `index` is set to `0` -- the orchestrator replaces it with the correct session index (see \"Index assignment\" below).\n\n2. `suppressAssistantResponse: true` hides the AI's follow-up. The AI still receives the result string (so it has context for follow-ups), but the client does not see the AI echoing \"100 miles equals 160.93 km.\"\n\n3. On error, the executor returns a plain string. This lets the AI explain what went wrong in its own words -- \"I could not convert miles to knots because they measure different things.\"\n\n## Adding Client Messages\n\nIf the tool wants to send a custom message to the client, use `clientMessages`. Any valid `OutgoingMessage` type works -- `entry_upsert`, `entry_delta`, `entry_commit`, or `error`.","is_error":false}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"fd002503-12d1-4a91-8dda-ba6311aa517b","uuid":"a5ea21f9-a51a-4a4e-b960-c0ecfcb022c7","timestamp":"2026-11-05T18:58:43.033Z","tool_use_result":{"stdout":"# Tool Responses\n\n| Field  | Value |\n| ------ | ----- |\n| Issue  | n/a   |\n| Status | Draft |\n\nBy default, a tool executor returns a plain string that feeds back into the AI conversation. Two gates in that job are missing from it because both diff against\n`origin/main` and neither runs the same way on a checkout: the spec anchor check\nand the changelog check.\n\nTwo further CI jobs are worth running locally before a release or a change that\ntouches packaging: `npm run check:build-chain` (audit and action pins) and\n`npm run smoke` (packs the tarball and installs it outside this tree).\n\n## Spec Header Table\n\nEvery `specs/*/spec.md` opens with its title, then a two-column header table,\nand carries a lead paragraph of prose before its first `##` section:\n\n```markdown\n# <spec title>\n\n| Field  | Value                  |\n| ------ | ---------------------- |\n| Issue  | re-cinq/HALEngine#<n> |\n| Status | Draft                  |\n\n<lead paragraph>\n```\n\nThe lead paragraph does not have to sit immediately after the table: a spec\ncarrying a metadata block of its own may place that block between the two. What\nthe convention requires is that prose, rather than a section heading, follows\nthe header material, and that the prose runs to at least 40 characters -\nanything shorter is reported as no lead paragraph at all.\n\n`Issue` names the issue the spec was written against, or `n/a` for the specs\nthat predate this convention.\n\n`Status` is one of `Draft`, `In Progress` or `Shipped`. It is not a mood, and\nit is not a claim about how finished the feature is: it is the spec's own\ntest-citation coverage. No testable statement cited is `Draft`, some cited is\n`In Progress`, all cited is `Shipped`. A spec describing shipped, working\nbehaviour still reads `Draft` until its statements cite the tests that\nvalidate them.\n\nA spec that should no longer be graded takes a terminal value instead. The\nparser buckets roughly sixteen labels into five buckets, and the two terminal\nones skip the coverage check whatever the citation count:\n\n| Written into the spec                                            | Bucket                       |\n| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |\n| `Draft`                                                          | `draft`                      |\n| `In Progress`, `In Review`, `Planning`, `WIP`, `Proposed`        | `in-progress`                |\n| `Shipped`, `Implemented`, `Complete`, `Accepted`, `Done`, `Live` | `shipped`                    |\n| `Retired`, `Superseded`, `Removed`, `Deprecated`, `Obsolete`     | `retired` - skips the check  |\n| `Rejected`, `Abandoned`                                          | `rejected` - skips the check |\n\nPrefer the canonical `Draft` / `In Progress` / `Shipped` for a live spec; reach\nfor `Retired` or `Rejected` rather than leaving a superseded spec to claim a\ncoverage tier it will never earn.\n\nADRs do not carry this table. They declare their state as YAML frontmatter\n`status:` instead - `accepted` for a decision the code implements, `proposed`\nfor one it does not. That field does mean maturity, which the spec `Status` row\nexplicitly does not. The difference is deliberate: ADRs are exempt from the\ncoverage tier, because asking a decision record to cite a test for every\nstatement it makes is the wrong ask of a decision record.\n\n`.specify/spec.md` is exempt from this section. It is the repo-level system\nspec, it predates the convention, and its content is deliberately frozen -\ngiving it a header table and a lead paragraph would mean writing new prose into\na file that is meant to stay unchanged. The exemption covers the header table\nand the lead paragraph only: the Lore coverage job does scan\n`.specify/spec.md`, so link placement still applies to it.\n\n## Spec Test Links\n\nStatements in `specs/*/spec.md` cite their validating test in a trailing\nparenthetical at the end of the statement, where a list item counts as one\nstatement and a paragraph counts per sentence. Tests live beside their source\nin this repo, so the path points into `src/`:\n\n```markdown\n- All entries within a single assistant response are committed before the next\n  user message is processed\n  ([validated by: commits every entry before the next user message](../../src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.test.ts#L42)).\n```\n\nThe citation carries the test's **name** as well as its line. The name is what the\nauthor cited; the line is a derived pointer, and it goes stale on its own - adding\nan import above a suite moves every test below it, and the citation lands on a\ndifferent, still-valid declaration without anything noticing. `npm run spec:names`\nholds each citation to the test it names, and `npm run spec:names:fix` repoints the\nline from the name. The `#Lnn` stays because the lint rule and the coverage job\nboth index by it; a citation without one marks the whole file covered rather than\none test.\n\nA citation counts as coverage only where it is trailing, and a test link placed\nanywhere else in the statement is a misplaced citation rather than a weaker one.\nUpstream `check:spec-links` reports it and exits 1, and the coverage job that\nconsumes these specs records nothing for it - so a spec can read as fully cited while its coverage is\nzero. A mid-statement link to something that is not a test file - a script, a\ndoc, another spec - is ordinary prose, is never reported, and was never coverage\nto begin with. A misplaced citation is fixed by moving it to the end of its\nstatement, never by deleting it.\n\nIn a test file the `#Lnn` anchor must land on the `it(`, `test(` or `describe(`\ndeclaration itself - not a blank line, not one holding only closing punctuation,\nand not a line inside the test body. A citation onto an `expect` renders and\nresolves like any other, and proves nothing: no reader can turn that line back\ninto the name of a case. `scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs` reports all four as\n`rotten` and exits 1 in both modes. A citation into a file that is not a test -\na workflow, a config, `package.json` - has no declaration to land on and is held\nonly to existing and carrying content.\n\nWhat no gate can catch is an anchor aimed at the wrong declaration: a real but\nunintended `it(` passes every check. The tell is that the test the statement\nmeant to cite goes on reading as uncited in the `require-spec-link` backlog.\n\nAnchors drift silently whenever a cited file gains or loses lines above them, so\nafter editing any cited file re-run `node scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs`\nrather than hand-correcting the numbers.
